source_text: Summus igitur deus ac parens omnium cum religionem suam transferre uoluisset, doctorem iustitiae misit e caelo, ut nouis cultoribus nouam legem in eo uel per eum daret, non sicut ante fecerat per hominem, sed tamen nasci eum uoluit tamquam hominem, ut per omnia summo patri similis existeret. ipse enim pater deus, origo et principium rerum, quo-niam parentibus caret, ὰπάπωρ atque ὰμήτωρ a Trismegisto uerissime nominatur, quod ei nullo sit procreatus. idcirco etiam filium bis nasci oportuit, ut et ipse fieret ὰπάτωρ atque ὰμήτωρ. in prima enim natiuitate spiritali ὰμήτωρ fuit, quia sine officio matris a solo deo patre generatus est, in secunda uero carnali ὰπάτωρ fuit, quoniam sine patris officio uirginali utero procreatus est, ut mediam inter deum hominemque substantiam gerens nostram hanc fragilem inbecillamque naturam quasi manu ad inmortalitatem posset educere. factus est et dei filius per spiritum et hominis per carnem, id est et deus et homo. dei uirtus in eo ex operibus quae fecit apparuit, fragilitas hominis ex passione quam pertulit: quam cur susceperit paulo post docebo. interim et deum fuisse et hominem ex utroque genere permixtum prophetis uaticinantibus discimus. Esaias deum fuisse testatur his uerbis: fatigata est Aegyptus, et negotiatio Aethiopum et Sabain uiri alti ad te transgredientur et tui erunt serui et post te ambulabunt uincti conpedibus et adorabunt te et in te precabuntur: quoniam in te deus est, et non est deus alius praeter te. tu enim es deus, et nos nesciebamus, deus Israhel saluator. confundentur et reuerebuntur omnes qui aduersantur tibi, et cadent in confessionem. item propheta Hieremias sic ait: hic deus noster est et non deputabitur alius absque illo, qui inuenit omnem uiam prudentiae et dedit eam Iacob puero suo et Israhel dilecto sibi. post haec in terris uisus est et cum hominibus conuersatus est. item Dauid in psalmo XLEQI: thronus tuus, deus, in saecula saeculorum, uirga aequitatis uirga regni tui. dilexisti iustitiam, odio habuisti iniustitiam. propterea unxit te dominus deus tuus oleum exultationis. quo uerbo etiam nomen ostendit, siquidem, ut supra docui, ab unctione appellatus est Christus. deinde hominem fuisse eundem Hieremias docet dicens: et homo est et quis cognouit eum? item Esaias: et mittet eis dominus hominem, qui saluabit eos et iudicans sanabit eos.
thought_title: God's Son as Teacher of Justice
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, the highest God and parent of all, when he wanted to transfer his own religion, sent a teacher of justice from heaven, so that he might give a new law to new cultivators in him or through him, not as he had done before through a man, but nevertheless he wanted him to be born as a man, so that he might exist as similar to the highest Father in all things. For the Father God himself, the origin and principle of things, since he lacks parents, is most truly called ἀπάτωρ and ἀμήτωρ by Trismegistus, because he was not produced by anyone. Therefore, it was also necessary for the Son to be born twice, so that he himself might become ἀπάτωρ and ἀμήτωρ. For in the first spiritual birth, he was ἀμήτωρ, because he was generated by God the Father alone without the service of a mother, in the second truly carnal birth, he was ἀπάτωρ, because he was produced from a virginal womb without the service of a father, so that bearing a middle substance between God and man, he might lead our fragile and weak nature to immortality as if by hand. And he became both the Son of God through the Spirit and the son of man through flesh, that is, both God and man. The power of God appeared in him from the works that he did, the fragility of man from the passion that he endured, which I will explain why he undertook a little later. Meanwhile, we learn from prophesying prophets that he was both God and man, mixed from both kinds. Isaiah testifies that he was God with these words: Egypt has been weakened, and the merchandise of the Ethiopians and the Sabeans, men of great stature, will pass over to you and will be your servants, and they will walk behind you in fetters and will adore you and will pray to you, because God is in you, and there is no other God besides you. For you are God, and we did not know, God of Israel, Savior. And all who oppose you will be confounded and will reverence and will fall into confession. Likewise, the prophet Jeremiah says thus: This is our God, and no other will be regarded apart from him, who found all the way of wisdom and gave it to Jacob, his servant, and Israel, his beloved. After these things, he was seen on earth and conversed with men. Likewise, David in Psalm 45 says: Your throne, God, is forever and ever, the scepter of your kingdom is a scepter of equity. You loved justice, you hated iniquity. Therefore, the Lord your God anointed you with the oil of gladness. By which word, he also shows his name, since, as I taught above, he was called Christ from anointing. Then Jeremiah teaches that he was the same man, saying: And he is a man, and who knows him? Likewise, Isaiah: And the Lord will send them a man who will save them and judging will heal them.

bible_refs.note: et homo est et quis cognouit eum

pass_b_english: Therefore the highest God, the parent of all, decided to transfer his religion and so sent a teacher of justice from heaven, that he might give a new law to new worshipers in him or through him — not as he had done before through a man, yet still he willed him to be born as a man so that he might exist as wholly like the highest Father. For God the Father himself, the origin and principle of all things, lacks parents; therefore Trismegistus most truly names him ἀπάτωρ and ἀμήτωρ, because he was not generated by anyone. For this reason the Son also had to be born twice, that he himself might become ἀπάτωρ and ἀμήτωρ. In his first, spiritual birth he was ἀμήτωρ, because he was begotten by God the Father alone without a mother’s role; in his second, carnal birth he was ἀπάτωρ, because he was born from a virgin’s womb without a father’s role, so that, bearing a middle substance between God and man, he might lead this fragile, weak nature of ours by the hand toward immortality. He became the Son of God through the Spirit and the son of man through flesh — that is, both God and man. God’s power shone forth in him from the works he did; man’s frailty appeared in the passion he endured — why he undertook it I will explain shortly. Meanwhile, from the prophets we learn that he was both God and man, compounded of both natures. Isaiah testifies that he was God in these words: “Egypt has been exhausted, and the trade of the Ethiopians and the Sabeans, men of stature, will come over to you and become your servants; they will walk behind you in chains, they will worship you and pray to you, because God is in you, and there is no other God besides you. For you are God, though we did not know it, God of Israel, Savior. All who oppose you will be put to shame and will reverence you, and they will fall in confession” (Isaiah). Likewise Jeremiah says: “This is our God, and no other will be reckoned apart from him, who found every way of wisdom and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After these things he was seen on earth and conversed with men” (Jeremiah). Likewise David in Psalm 45: “Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever; the scepter of your kingdom is a scepter of equity. You loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness” (Psalm 45). By this word he also shows his name, since, as I taught above, he was called Christ from the anointing. Then Jeremiah teaches that the same one was a man, saying: “And he is a man — who can know him?” (Jeremiah). Likewise Isaiah: “And the Lord will send them a man who will save them, and judging will heal them” (Isaiah).

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the theological nuances of the Latin, specifically the distinction between the two births (spiritual/apatōr and carnal/amētōr) and the dual nature of Christ. Scripture citations in Pass B correctly identify the books (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Psalm 45) and include the required inline parenthetical citations for the quoted/alluded clauses, even though specific verse numbers are not provided in the source. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Locked Latin.
